strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing: applying dual curriculum design/learnability directly in the partner-policy space, with a clean conceptual unification showing E3T (fixed epsilon), FCP/MEP (static populations) as special cases of the proposed framework.

Comprehensive empirical program: five Overcooked-AI layouts, strong population-based and population-free baselines (SP, FCP, MEP, E3T), two ablations, four learnability functions, a human user study, and a joint level-partner variant (JUPD) on the OGC. UPD achieves the best average return in all reported tables.

The human-AI user study is a valuable and relatively rare addition; it reports significant effects on both return and subjective measures (adaptivity, human-likeness, collaboration, frustration) with proper Holm-Bonferroni correction and Cronbach's alpha for aggregation.

Practical significance: the population-free design avoids the large compute overhead of pretrained populations, and the JUPD integration shows the method plugs into existing UED (SFL) at essentially no extra cost.
Reproducibility is well handled: code is released, hyperparameter tables and search ranges are given, six seeds are used, and the infrastructure/compute requirements are documented.

The limitations section is honest and specific (discrete action spaces, restricted behavioural diversity, agent-agent vs. human-agent gap), and the emergent convention-breaking behaviour is an interesting qualitative finding.
weaknesses: The paper's central novel component—learnability-based partner selection—is only weakly supported empirically. The ablation 'UPD w/o l' (which removes the learnability scoring entirely) reaches 90.0 average vs. 94.4 for full UPD, with largely overlapping standard deviations, and on 4 of 5 layouts (CRoom 106.9 vs 108.1, CR 68.9 vs 69.2, CC 64.5 vs 64.5, FC 45.7 vs 48.7) the difference is within noise; the advantage is essentially driven by the AA layout. This undercuts the claim that adaptive, learnability-driven curricula are the decisive mechanism.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the main agent-agent results (Tables 1 and 2). Given the large per-layout variance and only six seeds, it is difficult to judge whether the reported rankings are robust rather than seed noise.

The 'first method' claims (fully unsupervised joint level-partner curriculum; population-free AHT) are stated strongly but not sharply differentiated from closely related concurrent work (e.g., Wang et al. 2025 ROTATE regret-driven open-ended AHT training; You et al. 2025 automatic curriculum for zero-shot coordination), which are cited but not directly compared or discussed as competing claims to the same novelty.

The human study is small (n=12) and covers only three layouts with 36 games per method; while the effects are significant, the sample limits generalizability, and the paper does not report per-question effect sizes or discuss power.

The authors themselves caution that Tables 1 and 2 are not directly comparable due to observation differences between Overcooked-AI and the OGC, which limits the strength of the cross-setting conclusions.
The claim of 'emergent convention-breaking' (Figure 4) is intriguing but supported only by qualitative observation with no controlled analysis or quantitative link to improved zero-shot coordination.

strengths: The core conceptual framing is genuinely novel and interesting: applying dual curriculum design (DCD) directly to the space of partner policies, and reinterpreting E3T, FCP, and MEP as special cases with fixed generators or static populations, is a clean and useful way to organise the AHT literature.

The empirical breadth is substantial: five Overcooked-AI layouts, six seeds, four baselines, two ablations, four learnability-function variants, and a separate joint partner-environment experiment on the OGC with six seeds. The authors also gave baselines more compute (2x steps, per-layout LR tuning) rather than less, which strengthens the fairness of the comparison.

The human user study is a real differentiator. A within-subjects design with 12 participants and 36 games per method, correct statistics (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction, one-sided paired t-tests, Cronbach's alpha = 0.938), double-blind agent identity, and reported ethics approval is more rigorous than typical agent-only AHT evaluations.

Reproducibility is generally well handled: detailed hyperparameters, network architecture, infrastructure, hyperparameter search ranges, and a stated code release (though the URL appears truncated in the supplied text).

The discussion is honest about limitations (discrete action space, limited behavioural diversity of the generator) and flags the important finding that agent-agent rankings (MEP vs. E3T) do not always match human-agent rankings.
weaknesses: The paper's headline contribution - learnability-based partner selection - shows only marginal and likely non-significant gains. UPD (94.4 average) versus the UPD w/o learnability ablation (90.0 average) differs by ~4.4 points with standard deviations of ~8-11 across six seeds, i.e., within noise. The paper itself concedes that 'the online partner generator alone induces a natural curriculum,' which undercuts the central claim that adaptive selection is what makes the method work.

No statistical significance testing is reported for the main results (Tables 1 and 2) despite repeated claims that UPD 'consistently outperforms' baselines and ablations. Given overlapping error bars (e.g., UPD vs. E3T in CRoom, UPD vs. UPD w/o bias in several layouts), these claims are not adequately supported by the evidence as presented.

The variance-based learnability score l_var is conceptually confounded. Partners are stochastic policies (mixtures with a uniform-random policy), so return variance across N=10 rollouts conflates the partner's own action stochasticity with the ego agent's learning frontier. A partner could score highly simply for being noisy rather than for being informative, which weakens the theoretical justification that variance tracks learnability in the continuous-reward case.

The CV^2 formulation used for the joint setting normalises variance by the squared mean. As the mean return approaches zero (near-unsolvable or extremely hard levels/partners), CV^2 can blow up, which would tend to prioritise exactly the pathological hardest cases the authors elsewhere argue cause training collapse. The paper does not reconcile this tension or justify why CV^2 is a valid learnability proxy.

Several claims are overstated relative to the method. The abstract advertises training 'without manual parameter tuning,' yet UPD has multiple tuned hyperparameters (buffer size, N, Dirichlet alpha, refresh frequency) selected via the search ranges in Table 4. Similarly, the 'first method enabling fully unsupervised curricula over both level and partner distributions' is a strong priority claim that is hard to verify from the manuscript.

The E3T baseline is fixed at epsilon = 0.5 (and 0.0 for FC) with no per-layout or per-stage tuning. Since UPD's practical advantage over E3T is largely automatic adaptation of epsilon, the comparison risks being a strawman: a well-tuned fixed-epsilon E3T (the strongest population-free competitor) is not evaluated, so it is unclear how much of the gain is due to the method versus the absence of tuning in the baseline.

The evaluation populations are constructed by the authors (BRDiv, human-inspired heuristics, hardcoded, random). While they describe mitigations, the risk remains that the population is chosen in a way that flatters UPD, and the per-layout partner counts (4-9) and their composition are not ablated.

Some qualitative claims, such as 'emergent convention-breaking' from directional-bias shifts (Figure 4), are supported only by visual inspection of aggregate curves without quantitative analysis, and are presented more strongly in the abstract than the evidence warrants.

strengths: Introduces a novel and general framework, UPD, that applies dual curriculum design to the partner-policy space, enabling population-free adaptive partner generation and unifying prior AHT methods such as E3T, FCP, and MEP as special cases.

Proposes a flexible partner generator combining variable mixing and Dirichlet-biased randomisation, together with a variance-based learnability selection mechanism; the integration with SFL (JUPD) enables joint unsupervised curricula over both levels and partners.

Provides comprehensive empirical evidence: five Overcooked-AI layouts, six seeds, strong population-based and population-free baselines, ablations, and OGC experiments where JUPD outperforms DR-DR, CEC, and SFL-E3T.

Includes a double-blind human user study (12 participants, 144 games) with Holm-Bonferroni-corrected tests showing UPD achieves higher returns and is rated significantly more adaptive, human-like, collaborative, and less frustrating.

Offers useful analyses of emergent behaviours, including layout-dependent epsilon dynamics, convention/symmetry breaking in partner biases, and learnability landscapes, and discusses limitations honestly.
Reproducibility is generally good: detailed hyperparameters, architecture, seeds, compute infrastructure, code availability, and ethics approval/informed consent are reported.
weaknesses: The variance-based learnability score ℓ_var is heuristic and not rigorously justified; high return variance can reflect stochasticity/noise rather than the learning frontier. The claim that it prepares agents for both best- and worst-case partners is questionable because variance is low for consistent success or failure. Moreover, the ablation UPD w/o ℓ performs nearly as well (90.0 vs 94.4 average), so the contribution of learnability selection is modest and not statistically tested.

Several experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing or unclear: rollout length L for partner scoring, p_bias, the number of partner sampling iterations per training loop, and how partner evaluation rollouts are counted in the reported total timesteps. The claim that JUPD adds no computational cost beyond parameter sampling is not fully supported.

Artificial-agent results are reported as mean ± std over six seeds without significance tests, and several UPD-vs-ablation/baseline differences are small on layouts such as CR and CC, weakening the 'consistently outperforms' claim. No comparison to recent AHT methods such as ROTATE (2025) or other curriculum-based AHT approaches is provided.
The human study, while valuable, uses only 12 participants; order and learning effects are randomised but not explicitly modelled, and per-layout or per-partner human analyses are limited.

The causal interpretation of emergent convention-breaking and symmetry breaking in generated partners is speculative; the link between these phenomena and improved ad-hoc teamwork performance is not isolated experimentally.

The term 'population-free' may be somewhat misleading because UPD maintains a buffer of 512 generated partners and samples 8192 candidates per loop; it is population-free only in the sense of avoiding pretrained partners.

strengths: Clean and original conceptual framing: the paper recasts partner policies as induced training environments (Eqs. 2-4) and applies the learnability/SFL machinery from UED to the partner space, which is a genuinely new and sensible axis of curriculum design.

Comprehensive empirical effort: 282 trained policies across Level-Based Foraging, five Overcooked-AI layouts, the Overcooked Generalisation Challenge, and a double-blind human-AI user study, with 6 seeds for the main comparisons and per-layout analyses of selection dynamics (Figures 4-6).

Practical value: UPD removes the need for pre-trained partner populations and for the task-specific epsilon tuning that limits E3T, and it reports a single shared hyperparameter set across all Overcooked layouts.

The joint extension (JUPD) to partner-and-level curricula in the procedurally generated OGC is a natural and useful contribution, achieving the best average return against DR-DR, CEC, and SFLE3T (Table 2).

The human study is methodologically reasonable for this literature: within-subjects design, randomised ordering, double-blind, Cronbach's alpha reported, and one-sided paired tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction.

Honest limitations discussion and a transparency note about previously corrected baseline experiments; ablations (w/o bias, w/o learnability) and sensitivity analyses over alternative learnability functions (Figure 19) are included.
weaknesses: The central novelty - learnability-based partner selection - delivers only a modest gain over its own removal: UPD 94.4 vs. UPD w/o l 90.8 (Table 1), and the paper itself concedes that 'a large share of the AHT improvement ... appears to come from large-scale partner generation and biasing.' This weakens the headline claim that the learnability-driven curriculum is the key ingredient.

Mixed per-layout results undercut the robustness claims: in Table 3, ROTATE outperforms UPD on CRoom, CR, and FC, and UPD is below several baselines on CRoom even in Table 1; the aggregate win is partly driven by large margins on AA alone.

The theoretical grounding is loose. The paper leans on Foster et al. (2026) to argue that expected policy improvement scales with return variance, but this result is for a single-agent advantage-based setting; the transfer to the induced multi-agent game is asserted rather than carefully justified, and the empirical ablation (w/o l) suggests the practical signal is weak.

The human study, while well-designed, rests on only 12 participants (36 games per method); the authors acknowledge this limits the strength of conclusions, but several strong subjective claims (more human-like, less frustrating) are made from this small sample.

Baseline fairness/competitiveness is not fully settled: the transparency note indicates earlier baseline misconfiguration that had to be corrected, and it is unclear how much residual tuning differences (e.g., MEP tuned per layout, ROTATE reused from prior work with only 3 seeds) affect the comparison.

Presentation issues: several figures (e.g., Figure 5 and the algorithm boxes) have overlapping/cluttered text, and the partner-scoring equation in Algorithm 1 line 8 is self-referential/undefined, making the exact selection procedure hard to verify.

The partner generator, while described as general, is a specific epsilon-mixture with Dirichlet bias; the paper does not establish how sensitive the method is to the choice of generator (only the bias ablation is provided), so the 'framework' claim is broader than the evidence.

strengths: Novel and clean conceptual framing: treating a partner policy π_p as inducing a training environment G_{π_p,θ} (Eqs. 2–4) and applying learnability-based selection over the *partner* space, rather than only over level parameters, is a genuinely new and natural extension of UED to ad-hoc teamwork.

Broad empirical validation: 282 trained policies across Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked-AI, and the Overcooked Generalisation Challenge, plus a human-AI user study with appropriate statistics (one-sided Wilcoxon/paired t-tests, Holm-Bonferroni correction, Cronbach's α = 0.916 for the composite score). UPD is reported to outperform E3T and population-based baselines (Table 1: UPD 94.4 vs E3T 78.8, MEP 75.3, FCP 70.0) with a single hyperparameter set across layouts.

The joint extension (JUPD) is a meaningful contribution: it addresses a documented gap (Ruhdorfer et al., 2025b) where existing AHT methods do not scale to procedurally generated, under-specified levels, and it improves over SFLE3T (58.9 vs 44.0 avg in Table 2).

The convention-selection analysis (Sec. 4.4, Appendix C) and the emergent convention-breaking observation (Fig. 6) are interesting and supported by the UPD w/o ℓ ablation (Fig. 21), showing that bias-switching dynamics arise from the generation+selection interaction rather than from the generator alone.

Commendable honesty: the ablation (UPD w/o bias, UPD w/o ℓ) is reported transparently, the limitations section candidly discusses the compute trade-off and that learnability provides only 'additional gain', and a transparency note discloses that baselines had implementation issues that were corrected.
weaknesses: The headline mechanism is not clearly the driver. The paper's framing centers on learnability-based partner selection, yet UPD (94.4 ± 2.3) is statistically indistinguishable from UPD w/o ℓ (90.8 ± 6.0) in Table 1 (overlapping error bars, no significance test), and the authors themselves state 'a large share of the AHT improvement thus appears to come from large-scale partner generation and biasing.' This undercuts the 'Unsupervised Partner Design' claim and suggests the main novelty (learnability) is a minor add-on.

Incremental novelty. Each component is borrowed: E3T partner mixing (with ε randomized), Dirichlet bias masking, and SFL's learnability criterion (Rutherford et al., 2024). The contribution is essentially a recombination, and the strongest part (random-ε + bias + large-scale parallel generation) is a modification of E3T rather than a new principle.

Theoretical grounding is loose. Sec. 4.1 cites Foster et al. (2026) to argue expected policy improvement is proportional to the variance of the learning signal, but UPD uses variance of *returns* (Eq. 5), not the advantage/learning signal used in PPO — the claimed proportionality does not directly carry over, and this gap is not addressed.

The 'removing manual parameter tuning' claim is overstated: UPD introduces several new hyperparameters (|B|, N, R, ρ, α, p_bias), and Table 3 shows fine-tuned UPD reaches 102.3 vs 94.4 for the shared config, indicating layout-specific tuning still helps materially.

The OGC comparison conflates generation and selection: JUPD differs from SFLE3T both in partner generation (random ε + bias vs fixed ε = 0.5) and in selection, so the source of the 44.0 → 58.9 gain cannot be attributed to learnability-driven partner design.

Reproducibility gaps: the project page/code link is blanked out in the submission, and the transparency note reveals earlier baseline implementation/configuration errors, which raises questions about the reliability of the reported baseline comparisons. The LBF margin over the best E3T (≈0.31 vs 0.28) is small with overlapping error bars and no significance testing.

The human study rests on a small sample (12 participants, 36 games per method), which the authors acknowledge; the per-question significance claims and the composite-preference conclusions are correspondingly fragile.

strengths: Introduces a novel and natural extension of unsupervised environment design to the partner space: using learnability-based scoring to adaptively generate and select training partners. This is a clean conceptual contribution for population-free ad-hoc teamwork.

Strong empirical evaluation across three settings: Level-Based Foraging, Overcooked-AI, and the Overcooked Generalisation Challenge. UPD achieves the best average return in Table 1 (94.4) and JUPD achieves the best average in Table 2 (58.9), outperforming both population-based and population-free baselines.

Includes a double-blind human-AI user study (12 participants, 144 games) with appropriate statistical testing and Holm-Bonferroni correction. UPD agents obtain higher returns and are rated as more adaptive, more human-like, and less frustrating than SP, MEP, and E3T baselines.

Comprehensive ablations and analyses: UPD w/o bias, UPD w/o learnability, alternative learnability functions (Fig. 19), per-partner results (Fig. 20), and curriculum dynamics (Figs. 4-6, 16-18) provide insight into why and when the method works.

Practical efficiency analysis in Appendix F argues that UPD's online partner scoring can be cheaper than population-based pretraining in vectorised JAX simulators, and the paper provides extensive hyperparameter tables and training curves.

The method extends naturally to joint partner-environment curricula (JUPD) with a coefficient-of-variation correction, showing robustness in procedurally generated settings where classic AHT methods are difficult to scale.
Limitations and broader impact are discussed explicitly, and the human study follows ethics approval, informed consent, and compensation guidelines.
weaknesses: The 'population-free' framing is somewhat overstated: UPD maintains a buffer of |B| = 512 partner policies and samples 4000 candidates per refresh, which is effectively an online population. It avoids pre-trained populations and a separate population-training stage, but it is not population-free in the literal sense.

The learnability component is not decisively responsible for the main gains. In Table 1, UPD w/o learnability already achieves 90.8 average vs. 94.4 for full UPD, and the authors acknowledge that large-scale partner generation and biasing may drive much of the improvement. This weakens the central claim that learnability-based partner selection is the key mechanism.

The theoretical justification for using return variance as the learnability score is thin. The paper cites Foster et al. (2026) to argue that expected one-step improvement scales with variance in an induced single-agent game, but does not formally derive or empirically isolate this connection for the multi-agent partner-selection setting.

Baseline tuning may not be fully equalised. E3T uses reported hyperparameters (e.g., epsilon = 0.5 for most Overcooked layouts) rather than being tuned for this evaluation protocol; MEP is tuned per layout; ROTATE is run with 3 seeds vs. UPD's 6 seeds. Moreover, UPD (fine-tuned) in Table 3 uses per-layout hyperparameters and improves substantially, complicating claims about a single configuration.

The human study has a small sample (12 participants, 36 games per method). The authors appropriately note this limitation, but significance claims and preference ratings should still be interpreted cautiously.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the project page URL is blank in the appendix ('available at .'), and the transparency note states that an earlier version had implementation/config issues affecting baseline experiments that required reruns. Although corrected, this raises some confidence concerns.

Presentation has avoidable issues, including Algorithm 1 line 8 with a redundant placeholder ('Compute: ℓ(π_ego, π_p, θ) = ℓ(π_ego, π_p, θ)'), awkward equation numbering and section references, and missing URL information.

The OGC experiments use only the 5x5 version and a limited set of baselines (DR-DR, CEC, SFLE3T); no comparison to other UED methods (e.g., PLR, ACCEL) or ROTATE in the joint partner-level setting is provided, so the joint-curriculum claim is less thoroughly benchmarked than the fixed-environment claim.

The claim that UPD removes manual parameter tuning is qualified: UPD still has several hyperparameters (buffer size, N, R, alpha, rho, p_bias), and Table 5 shows that per-layout tuning can yield significant gains.
